macro.regime: Resilient risk-on vs. hawkish/geopolitical crosscurrents -- Fed/BOJ hikes absorbed, but oil's own price action now disagrees with the supply-shock narrative and the Xi-Trump summit remains a live binary risk
macro.narrative: The underlying regime is unchanged in its Fed/BOJ dimension -- both hikes (Fed to 3.75-4.00% under Chair Warsh, BOJ to 1.25%) were absorbed calmly, with the S&P/Nasdaq closing at/near records Friday and VIX falling a fifth straight session to 14.81. Oil is the one leg where the weekend's own price action undercut the headline narrative: a Houthi strike ignited an Aramco fuel-depot fire at Riyadh's main airport and Aramco cancelled all remaining September/October European crude allocations after the East-West pipeline went offline again, yet WTI futures fell further on Sunday's reopen ($100.30 to $95.92, -4.37%) rather than spiking on the supply cut -- consistent with OPEC/IEA cutting 2026 oil demand growth forecasts (Brent seen averaging ~$90/b in 2H26) and reports of refiners backfilling with North Sea/US WTI/Kazakh CPC barrels. Trump reportedly declined direct military support for Saudi Arabia against the Houthis before reportedly cutting a Camp David trip short and weighing a larger response -- the security-backstop question remains open even as the price signal has calmed. Separately, Beijing has warned it may cancel the Sept 23-24 Xi-Trump summit over a pending $14B Taiwan arms package, with Taiwan reporting elevated PLA aircraft/ship activity over the weekend -- a live, HK-tech-specific binary risk into this week, and China's own rare-earth export-control suspension is set to expire 2026-11-10, a second concrete date for that basket. Bitcoin holding near $81k on continued ETF inflows, with crypto's own Fear&Greed gauge (71, Greed) now diverging sharply from equities' CNN gauge (still in Fear), reads as a liquidity/momentum story independent of the broader risk backdrop. Net effect: the regime hasn't flipped, but oil's mixed signal argues for less conviction on the supply-shock trade than Sunday's read implied, while the summit remains the week's cleanest binary catalyst. Levels as of Fri 18 Sep US/HK/SGX/KR close (JPX closed today for a bank holiday) plus verified developments through Mon 21 Sep pre-open.

Precious metals extended their rally for a second day (GLD +0.71%, SLV +1.63%) and have shrugged off the hawkish Fed hike entirely, a structural signal reinforced by record central-bank gold buying and a sixth straight annual silver deficit. Oil is the genuinely unresolved leg: despite Aramco cancelling all Sept/Oct European allocations after the pipeline was forced offline again, WTI futures fell further on Sunday's reopen ($95.92, -4.37%) as OPEC/IEA's 2026 demand-growth downgrade and reported alternative-barrel backfill outweighed the supply-shock premium -- energy stays two-sided, not a clean long. Bank forecast ranges for silver remain unusually wide ($55-100/oz), reflecting high uncertainty.

BTC broke back above $80k into the weekend (a ~$81,193 live level, +6.3% Friday, not a close), with ETH (~$2,511, +4%) and SOL (~$106, +7.8%) also posting broad gains -- a more decisive move than the prior choppy, muted post-FOMC reaction. A hawkish Fed remains a structural liquidity headwind over 3-12 months, but the near-term price action has turned genuinely positive rather than merely stable.

10y Treasury yield held around 4.94-4.95% into Friday, stabilizing just below its pre-FOMC 19-year high rather than resuming its climb; the BOJ's softer-than-feared hike (JGB 10y yield actually fell ~5bp) removed a global-duration risk. Dot plot still signals at least one more 2026 hike, so duration risk stays elevated, but the immediate follow-through has been calmer than the hawkish dots alone would imply.

Fed funds at 3.75-4.00% with more hikes signaled, and the yen only modestly softer post-BOJ (156.64), keep the broad dollar bid intact and cash attractive on a risk-adjusted basis for a large cash pile; offsetting this is a medium-term credibility risk from visible, continuing political attacks on Fed independence.
